pluto.source: IAU 2015 (IAU north pole; Pluto rotates retrograde about it)

objects.name: Laniakea Supercluster

source.catalogue: Tully et al. 2014, Nature 513, 71
source.note: Marker placed toward the Great Attractor basin at an approximate centroid distance. Boundaries are schematic.

objects.info: A supercluster of roughly 100,000 galaxies defined by the flow field of galaxy velocities. It contains the Virgo Supercluster, hence the Local Group. Shown as a diffuse marker; the real boundary is a velocity-flow basin, not a sphere.

objects.name: Coma Cluster

source.catalogue: Cosmic Atlas bundled starter set (curated, approximate; cross-check with live SIMBAD/NED)

objects.info: A rich galaxy cluster with over 1,000 identified galaxies, dominated by two giant ellipticals (NGC 4874, NGC 4889). It lies in a different region of the sky from Virgo; it is a separate landmark, not nested inside Laniakea.

objects.name: Virgo Cluster

source.catalogue: Cosmic Atlas bundled starter set (curated, approximate; cross-check with live SIMBAD/NED)

objects.info: The nearest rich galaxy cluster, with ~1,300–2,000 member galaxies, including M87. The Local Group is a gravitationally infalling neighbour, not a member.

objects.name: Local Sheet

source.catalogue: Tully et al. 2008; McCall 2014
source.note: Schematic: a flattened planar structure ~23 Mly across, drawn as a marker centred near the Local Group.

objects.info: A thin planar structure of galaxies within about 7 Mpc, in which the Local Group is embedded. It is flattened; the marker here is only a label.

objects.name: Local Group

source.catalogue: McConnachie 2012, AJ 144, 4
source.note: Centre drawn between the Milky Way and M31 (barycentre is approximate).

objects.info: The galaxy group containing the Milky Way, Andromeda (M31), Triangulum (M33) and 80+ dwarf galaxies, ~10 million ly across.

objects.name: Milky Way Galaxy

source.catalogue: Bland-Hawthorn & Gerhard 2016, ARA&A 54, 529

objects.info: A barred spiral galaxy. The 3D model drawn here is an ILLUSTRATIVE procedural model (bulge, disk, four logarithmic arms) – not a measured map. The Sun is placed ~26,700 ly from the centre.

objects.name: Andromeda Galaxy (M31)

source.catalogue: Cosmic Atlas bundled starter set (curated, approximate; cross-check with live SIMBAD/NED)

objects.info: The nearest large spiral galaxy and the most massive member of the Local Group alongside the Milky Way. Approaching us at ~110 km/s.

objects.name: Triangulum Galaxy (M33)

source.catalogue: Cosmic Atlas bundled starter set (curated, approximate; cross-check with live SIMBAD/NED)

objects.info: The third-largest member of the Local Group; a spiral galaxy with active star formation.

objects.name: Orion Arm (Orion Spur)

source.catalogue: Xu et al. 2016, Sci. Adv. 2, e1600878 (maser parallaxes)
source.note: Drawn as a schematic line through the Sun; length ~20,000 ly, width ~3,500 ly.

objects.info: A minor spiral structure ("spur") between the Sagittarius and Perseus arms that hosts the Solar System. Its drawn path here is schematic.

objects.name: Carina Nebula

source.catalogue: Cosmic Atlas bundled starter set (curated, approximate; cross-check with live SIMBAD/NED)

objects.info: A large star-forming region in the Carina–Sagittarius arm hosting Eta Carinae and many massive stars. Drawn as an extended glow; structure is illustrative.

objects.name: Alnitak (Zeta Orionis)

source.catalogue: Cosmic Atlas bundled starter set (curated, approximate; cross-check with live SIMBAD/NED)

objects.info: Eastern star of Orion's Belt: a multiple system with a hot O-type supergiant. It is NOT physically close to the other belt stars along our line of sight.

objects.name: Alnilam (Epsilon Orionis)

source.catalogue: Cosmic Atlas bundled starter set (curated, approximate; cross-check with live SIMBAD/NED)

objects.info: Central belt star, a luminous blue supergiant. Its parallax distance is poorly constrained (~±20%).

objects.name: Mintaka (Delta Orionis)

source.catalogue: Cosmic Atlas bundled starter set (curated, approximate; cross-check with live SIMBAD/NED)

objects.info: Western belt star; a multiple system including an eclipsing binary.

objects.name: Betelgeuse (Alpha Orionis)

source.catalogue: Cosmic Atlas bundled starter set (curated, approximate; cross-check with live SIMBAD/NED)

objects.info: A colossal M-type red supergiant nearing the end of its nuclear life cycle. With a physical radius of ~764 solar radii (~3.55 AU), if placed at the centre of our Solar System its surface would engulf Mars and approach the orbit of Jupiter. It will eventually explode as a core-collapse Type II-P supernova.

objects.name: Pleiades (M45)

source.catalogue: Cosmic Atlas bundled starter set (curated, approximate; cross-check with live SIMBAD/NED)

objects.info: An open cluster of ~1,000 hot young stars dominated by luminous blue B-type stars. Unlike constellations, this IS a physical, gravitationally bound group embedded in a reflection nebula.

objects.name: Aldebaran (Alpha Tauri)

source.catalogue: Cosmic Atlas bundled starter set (curated, approximate; cross-check with live SIMBAD/NED)

objects.info: An orange giant star, the brightest in the constellation Taurus. Although it appears line-of-sight aligned with the Hyades cluster, it is a foreground star located ~65 ly away (~2.5× closer than the cluster).

objects.name: Sun

source.catalogue: NASA Solar System Exploration
source.note: Radius 695,700 km (0.00465 AU). Display radius exaggerated ~10×.

objects.info: The G2V star at the centre of the Solar System, ~26,673 ly from the Galactic Centre.

objects.name: Mercury

source.catalogue: JPL approximate Keplerian elements (1800–2050); NASA planetary fact sheets
source.note: Position is an approximate model, not JPL Horizons.

objects.info: 4,879 km diameter. Fastest planet; 88-day year.

objects.name: Venus

source.catalogue: JPL approximate Keplerian elements (1800–2050); NASA planetary fact sheets
source.note: Position is an approximate model, not JPL Horizons.

objects.info: Thick CO₂ atmosphere, hottest planet (~465 °C).

objects.name: Earth

source.catalogue: JPL approximate Keplerian elements (1800–2050); NASA planetary fact sheets
source.note: Position is an approximate model, not JPL Horizons.

objects.info: Our home planet; the only known world with life. Photorealistic scientific surface map with specular oceans and dynamic clouds.

objects.name: Mars

source.catalogue: JPL approximate Keplerian elements (1800–2050); NASA planetary fact sheets
source.note: Position is an approximate model, not JPL Horizons.

objects.info: Cold desert world with the largest volcano in the Solar System. Natural satellites: Phobos and Deimos.

objects.name: Jupiter

source.catalogue: JPL approximate Keplerian elements (1800–2050); NASA planetary fact sheets
source.note: Position is an approximate model, not JPL Horizons.

objects.info: Largest planet; gas giant with 95+ known moons including the four Galilean satellites.

objects.name: Saturn

source.catalogue: JPL approximate Keplerian elements (1800–2050); NASA planetary fact sheets
source.note: Position is an approximate model, not JPL Horizons.

objects.info: Gas giant with a prominent ring system and major moons including Titan and Enceladus.

objects.name: Uranus

source.catalogue: JPL approximate Keplerian elements (1800–2050); NASA planetary fact sheets
source.note: Position is an approximate model, not JPL Horizons.

objects.info: Ice giant rotating on its side (axial tilt 98°) with major moons Miranda, Ariel, Umbriel, Titania, Oberon.

objects.name: Neptune

source.catalogue: JPL approximate Keplerian elements (1800–2050); NASA planetary fact sheets
source.note: Position is an approximate model, not JPL Horizons.

objects.info: Outermost major planet: ice giant with supersonic winds and retrograde giant moon Triton.

objects.name: Moon

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris DE405/LE405); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Earth itself is placed at the Earth–Moon barycentre (existing planetary model, ~4,670 km offset ignored).

objects.info: Earth's only natural satellite, now drawn at its true distance (mean 384,400 km) on a mean-element Keplerian orbit with 6.0-yr apsidal and 18.6-yr nodal precession. Solar perturbations (evection, variation) are not modelled, so its position can be off by a few degrees.

objects.name: Phobos

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris MAR099); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Mean elements; Phobos's secular acceleration is not modelled (tens of km after decades).

objects.info: The larger, inner moon of Mars: an irregular, heavily cratered body dominated by the 9-km Stickney crater. It orbits below synchronous altitude, so it rises in the west on Mars and is slowly spiralling inward.

objects.name: Deimos

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris MAR099); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Mean elements with secular precession only; short-period perturbations ignored (see validation doc).

objects.info: The small outer moon of Mars. Its surface is smoothed by a thick regolith that fills in craters, giving it a softer look than Phobos.

objects.name: Io

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris JUP365); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Mean elements with secular precession only; short-period perturbations ignored (see validation doc).

objects.info: The most volcanically active body known. Tidal heating from its orbital resonance with Europa and Ganymede drives hundreds of active volcanoes; sulfur compounds colour its surface yellow, orange and red.

objects.name: Europa

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris JUP365); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Mean elements with secular precession only; short-period perturbations ignored (see validation doc).

objects.info: An ice-shelled moon with a global subsurface salt-water ocean. Its young, bright surface is crossed by long dark ridges and chaos terrain.

objects.name: Ganymede

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris JUP365); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Mean elements with secular precession only; short-period perturbations ignored (see validation doc).

objects.info: The largest moon in the Solar System, bigger than Mercury, and the only moon known to generate its own magnetic field. Dark ancient terrain is cut by bright grooved bands.

objects.name: Callisto

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris JUP365); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Mean elements with secular precession only; short-period perturbations ignored (see validation doc).

objects.info: The most heavily cratered body in the Solar System, with an old, dark surface and the huge Valhalla impact basin. It is outside the Io–Europa–Ganymede resonance and experiences little tidal heating.

objects.name: Amalthea

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris JUP365); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Mean elements with secular precession only; short-period perturbations ignored (see validation doc).

objects.info: The largest of Jupiter's inner moons: an elongated, very red, low-density body inside the orbit of Io that contributes dust to the gossamer ring.

objects.name: Thebe

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris JUP365); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Mean elements with secular precession only; short-period perturbations ignored (see validation doc).

objects.info: A small, dark, irregular inner moon whose debris feeds the outer gossamer ring.

objects.name: Metis

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris JUP365); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Mean elements with secular precession only; short-period perturbations ignored (see validation doc).

objects.info: The innermost known moon of Jupiter, orbiting inside the main ring faster than Jupiter rotates.

objects.name: Adrastea

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris JUP365); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: JPL lists a density of 0.90 ± 1.85 g/cm³ — not meaningful at this uncertainty, so it is not shown.

objects.info: A tiny moon at the outer edge of Jupiter's main ring. Its radius (8 ± 4 km) is very uncertain.

objects.name: Himalia

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris JUP347); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Ecliptic mean elements for a strongly Sun-perturbed orbit: errors of 10⁵–10⁶ km are expected (see validation doc).

objects.info: The largest irregular (captured) moon of Jupiter, on a distant, inclined and eccentric orbit strongly perturbed by the Sun.

objects.name: Elara

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris JUP347); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Ecliptic mean elements for a strongly Sun-perturbed orbit: errors of 10⁵–10⁶ km are expected.

objects.info: An irregular moon of the Himalia group. Its size is known only to ±25%.

objects.name: Mimas

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris SAT441); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Mean elements with secular precession only; short-period perturbations ignored (see validation doc).

objects.info: A small icy moon whose giant Herschel crater makes it resemble the Death Star. Its 2:1 resonance with ring particles clears the Cassini Division.

objects.name: Enceladus

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris SAT441); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Mean elements with secular precession only; short-period perturbations ignored (see validation doc).

objects.info: A brilliant white moon with a global subsurface ocean. Geysers at its south pole vent water vapour and ice that supply Saturn's E ring.

objects.name: Tethys

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris SAT441); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Mean elements with secular precession only; short-period perturbations ignored (see validation doc).

objects.info: An almost pure water-ice moon with the large Odysseus impact basin and the 2,000-km Ithaca Chasma canyon.

objects.name: Dione

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris SAT441); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Mean elements with secular precession only; short-period perturbations ignored (see validation doc).

objects.info: An icy moon whose trailing hemisphere is crossed by bright ice cliffs ("wispy terrain") formed by tectonic fracturing.

objects.name: Rhea

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris SAT441); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Mean elements with secular precession only; short-period perturbations ignored (see validation doc).

objects.info: Saturn's second-largest moon: a heavily cratered, icy body with a low density close to that of ice-rock mixtures.

objects.name: Titan

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris SAT441); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Mean elements with secular precession only; short-period perturbations ignored (see validation doc).

objects.info: Saturn's largest moon and the only moon with a thick atmosphere (1.5 bar, mostly nitrogen). Its orange haze hides methane lakes, rivers and dunes from visible-light view.

objects.name: Hyperion

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris SAT441); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Strong 4:3 resonance with Titan: mean elements can drift by 10⁴–10⁵ km.

objects.info: A highly porous, irregular moon with a sponge-like appearance. Its 4:3 resonance with Titan and elongated shape make its rotation chaotic.

objects.name: Iapetus

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris SAT441); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Mean elements with secular precession only; short-period perturbations ignored (see validation doc).

objects.info: A two-toned moon: its leading hemisphere is coated with dark material while the trailing hemisphere is bright ice. An equatorial ridge up to ~13 km high encircles part of it.

objects.name: Phoebe

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris SAT441); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Distant, Sun-perturbed retrograde orbit: errors of 10⁵ km or more are expected.

objects.info: A dark, retrograde, captured moon far outside the regular satellites. Dust from Phoebe forms the enormous Phoebe ring and probably darkened Iapetus's leading side.

objects.name: Janus

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris SAT415); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Mean elements with secular precession only; short-period perturbations ignored (see validation doc).

objects.info: A small inner moon of Saturn. Co-orbital with Epimetheus: the two swap orbits every ~4 years. Mean elements cannot represent the swap.

objects.name: Epimetheus

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris SAT415); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Mean elements with secular precession only; short-period perturbations ignored (see validation doc).

objects.info: A small inner moon of Saturn. Co-orbital with Janus: the two swap orbits every ~4 years. Mean elements cannot represent the swap.

objects.name: Pan

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris SAT415); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Mean elements with secular precession only; short-period perturbations ignored (see validation doc).

objects.info: A small inner moon of Saturn. Orbits inside the Encke Gap of the A ring, which it keeps open.

objects.name: Atlas

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris SAT415); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Mean elements with secular precession only; short-period perturbations ignored (see validation doc).

objects.info: A small inner moon of Saturn. Orbits just outside the A ring.

objects.name: Prometheus

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris SAT415); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Mean elements with secular precession only; short-period perturbations ignored (see validation doc).

objects.info: A small inner moon of Saturn. Inner shepherd of the F ring; chaotic interactions with Pandora.

objects.name: Pandora

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris SAT415); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Mean elements with secular precession only; short-period perturbations ignored (see validation doc).

objects.info: A small inner moon of Saturn. Outer shepherd of the F ring; chaotic interactions with Prometheus.

objects.name: Helene

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris SAT441); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Mean elements with secular precession only; short-period perturbations ignored (see validation doc).

objects.info: A small inner moon of Saturn. Trojan moon at Dione's leading L4 Lagrange point.

objects.name: Miranda

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris URA182); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Surface map is partial: Voyager 2 (1986) saw only the sunlit southern hemisphere. The north is shown as a neutral mean tone.

objects.info: A small moon with a patchwork of grooved coronae and the 20-km-deep Verona Rupes cliff — among the strangest landscapes in the Solar System.

objects.name: Ariel

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris URA182); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Surface map is partial: Voyager 2 (1986) saw only the sunlit southern hemisphere. The north is shown as a neutral mean tone.

objects.info: The brightest Uranian moon, with a relatively young surface cut by fault valleys (chasmata).

objects.name: Umbriel

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris URA182); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Surface map is partial: Voyager 2 (1986) saw only the sunlit southern hemisphere. The north is shown as a neutral mean tone.

objects.info: The darkest of Uranus's large moons, ancient and uniformly cratered, with a mysterious bright ring (Wunda) near its equator.

objects.name: Titania

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris URA182); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Surface map is partial: Voyager 2 (1986) saw only the sunlit southern hemisphere. The north is shown as a neutral mean tone.

objects.info: Uranus's largest moon, with huge fault canyons such as Messina Chasma that indicate past internal activity.

objects.name: Oberon

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris URA182); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Surface map is partial: Voyager 2 (1986) saw only the sunlit southern hemisphere. The north is shown as a neutral mean tone.

objects.info: The outermost large Uranian moon: old, heavily cratered, with dark material on some crater floors and a 11-km-high mountain.

objects.name: Puck

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris URA182); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Mean elements with secular precession only; short-period perturbations ignored (see validation doc).

objects.info: The largest of Uranus's small inner moons, discovered by Voyager 2 in 1985.

objects.name: Triton

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris NEP098); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Surface map is partial: Voyager 2 (1989) imaged mainly the southern hemisphere.

objects.info: Neptune's largest moon orbits RETROGRADE (opposite to Neptune's rotation), strong evidence that it is a captured Kuiper Belt object. Voyager 2 saw nitrogen geysers on its young surface.

objects.name: Nereid

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris NEP105); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: JPL lists GM = 0 for Nereid (mass not measured); shown as unknown.

objects.info: A moon on one of the most eccentric orbits known (e = 0.75), swinging from 1.4 to 9.7 million km from Neptune.

objects.name: Proteus

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris NEP098); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: The JPL density for Proteus (1.03 ± 0.97 g/cm³) is too uncertain to be shown.

objects.info: Neptune's second-largest moon: about as large as a body can be without being pulled round by its own gravity.

objects.name: Larissa

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris NEP098); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: JPL GM for this moon has an uncertainty larger than the value; mass shown as unknown.

objects.info: A small, dark inner moon of Neptune discovered by Voyager 2 in 1989.

objects.name: Galatea

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris NEP098); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: JPL GM for this moon has an uncertainty larger than the value; mass shown as unknown.

objects.info: A small, dark inner moon of Neptune discovered by Voyager 2 in 1989.

objects.name: Despina

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris NEP098); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: JPL GM for this moon has an uncertainty larger than the value; mass shown as unknown.

objects.info: A small, dark inner moon of Neptune discovered by Voyager 2 in 1989.

objects.name: Charon

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris PLU060); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Elements are the Pluto-centred relative orbit; positions are split about the barycentre with the JPL mass ratio (see ORBITAL_MECHANICS.md).

objects.info: Pluto's largest moon, half Pluto's diameter. Pluto and Charon orbit a common barycentre ~2,100 km above Pluto's surface, so they are often called a double dwarf planet.

objects.name: Styx

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris PLU060); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Elements treated as barycentric (circumbinary orbit). JPL masses for this moon are upper limits or highly uncertain.

objects.info: A small moon of Pluto orbiting the Pluto–Charon barycentre; imaged by New Horizons in 2015.

objects.name: Nix

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris PLU060); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Elements treated as barycentric (circumbinary orbit). JPL masses for this moon are upper limits or highly uncertain.

objects.info: A small moon of Pluto orbiting the Pluto–Charon barycentre; imaged by New Horizons in 2015.

objects.name: Kerberos

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris PLU060); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Elements treated as barycentric (circumbinary orbit). JPL masses for this moon are upper limits or highly uncertain.

objects.info: A small moon of Pluto orbiting the Pluto–Charon barycentre; imaged by New Horizons in 2015.

objects.name: Hydra

source.catalogue: JPL SSD Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (ephemeris PLU060); mean anomaly at epoch and mean motion fitted to JPL Horizons 2016–2036
source.note: Elements treated as barycentric (circumbinary orbit). JPL masses for this moon are upper limits or highly uncertain.

objects.info: A small moon of Pluto orbiting the Pluto–Charon barycentre; imaged by New Horizons in 2015.

objects.name: Pluto

source.catalogue: JPL SBDB osculating elements for 134340 Pluto, epoch JD 2457588.5 TDB (compared with the Pluto-system barycentre in Horizons)
source.note: Surface map is partial: the hemisphere facing New Horizons at closest approach is high-resolution, the far side is low-resolution and the south is unimaged.

objects.info: A dwarf planet in the Kuiper Belt with nitrogen glaciers, water-ice mountains and a thin hazy atmosphere. New Horizons flew past in 2015.

objects.name: Ceres

source.catalogue: JPL SBDB osculating elements, epoch JD 2461200.5 TDB (SPK-ID 20000001)
source.note: Two-body propagation of osculating elements ignores planetary perturbations; error grows with |t − epoch| (see validation doc).

objects.info: The largest object in the asteroid belt and the only dwarf planet in the inner Solar System. Dawn found briny carbonate deposits (Occator's bright spots) and evidence of a past or present subsurface brine layer.

objects.name: Vesta

source.catalogue: JPL SBDB osculating elements, epoch JD 2461200.5 TDB (SPK-ID 20000004)
source.note: Two-body propagation of osculating elements ignores planetary perturbations; error grows with |t − epoch| (see validation doc).

objects.info: The second-most-massive asteroid: a differentiated protoplanet with an iron core and basaltic crust. The giant Rheasilvia impact basin at its south pole is the source of the HED meteorites.

objects.name: Pallas

source.catalogue: JPL SBDB osculating elements, epoch JD 2461200.5 TDB (SPK-ID 20000002)
source.note: Two-body propagation of osculating elements ignores planetary perturbations; error grows with |t − epoch| (see validation doc).

objects.info: The third-largest asteroid, on a steeply inclined (35°) orbit. Its surface is heavily cratered, likely because of high-speed impacts on its tilted path.

objects.name: Hygiea

source.catalogue: JPL SBDB osculating elements, epoch JD 2461200.5 TDB (SPK-ID 20000010)
source.note: Two-body propagation of osculating elements ignores planetary perturbations; error grows with |t − epoch| (see validation doc).

objects.info: The fourth-largest asteroid and the largest of the dark C-type asteroids. VLT/SPHERE images show it is nearly spherical, making it a dwarf-planet candidate.

objects.name: Eris

source.catalogue: JPL SBDB osculating elements, epoch JD 2461200.5 TDB (SPK-ID 20136199)
source.note: Two-body propagation of osculating elements ignores planetary perturbations; error grows with |t − epoch| (see validation doc).

objects.info: The most massive known dwarf planet after Pluto and nearly the same size. Its discovery in 2005 led to the IAU definition of "dwarf planet".
